title: The harness picture
subject: How work gets done across the estate: who writes, where, with which credential, and where it lands

brief.background: Six registries now describe the harness: writers, venues, credentials, run methods, direct-to-main, and the joins between them. The Relations tab draws their schema, uniformly. This board looks for a designed picture of the structure itself, so that the owner can say for any agent or automation where it runs, what it signs in with, and where its work lands, and can judge which route to use to send work to Claude, Codex or Gemini.
brief.methodology: Eight concepts were written before any was judged, each differing in its **explanatory mechanism**: containment, flow, a credential-centred graph, metaphor, matrix, proportional flow, hierarchy, geography. Each had to carry the **one fact that should stand out**: five writers on the laptop share one git credential, while Claude in the cloud has its own. Data from `docs/writers.csv`, `docs/credentials.csv`, `docs/venues.csv`, `docs/run-methods.csv` and `docs/direct-to-main.csv` on web-tools#1197.

ideas.title: Security zones
ideas.commentary:
Machines as nested zones around you, with each credential a key on the zone's boundary.

It makes **where** vivid: the laptop is close, the clouds far. But concentric rings imply a ranking of trust the data does not record, and repos have no natural place.

ideas.title: Flow columns
ideas.commentary:
The Set tab's columns extended with a key column: what starts a writer, the writer, the key it writes with, where it lands.

Precise and already familiar from the Set tab, but a reader learns a row at a time; the shared laptop key is one box among many.

ideas.title: Key ring
ideas.commentary:
Each credential is a hub, with the writers that use it hanging off it and the repos it opens on the far side.

It makes the **shared laptop credential** impossible to miss. It loses where things run: the machine is only implied by which keys sit together.

ideas.title: Theatre
ideas.commentary:
Your own image: machines as stages, harnesses as costumes, models as the cast, credentials as props in hand.

Memorable and true to how the session reasoned, but a stage drawing cannot carry 18 writers and 7 keys legibly, and the metaphor needs explaining to anyone else.

ideas.title: Matrix
ideas.commentary:
Writers down the side, credentials and machines across, a dot where they meet.

Compact, complete and easy to check against the CSVs. It shows no direction or flow, so it answers lookup questions and not the question of how work moves.

ideas.title: Sankey
ideas.commentary:
Bands from what starts work, through machines and keys, to where it lands, each as wide as the writers on it.

It weighs things honestly (the laptop band is the widest), but individual writers disappear into bands, and with 18 writers the widths are small integers that read as noise.

ideas.title: Signature tree
ideas.commentary:
You at the top; beneath, the writers grouped by whose name their commits carry: you, Claude, or the workflow bot.

It answers attribution directly, which the Writes view cares about, but it hides machines and makes three of the seven keys look alike.

ideas.title: Hub map
ideas.commentary:
GitHub at the centre, where every write ends. Your machines on one side, the providers' on the other, each holding its writers; one road per credential runs into GitHub, as thick as the writers on it and labelled with whose name it signs.

It shows where, with what and whose name in one picture, and its two sides carry the one division the registries do not record: yours or a provider's.

grafts: machines as boxes that contain their writers
the credential as a node the writers converge on, so the shared laptop key reads at a glance
whose name each road's commits carry, written on its key
selection.rationale: The hub map answers all three questions in one picture without hiding a level: the writer sits in its machine, its line runs to its key, and the key's road into GitHub is as thick as the writers that share it. The key ring's convergence and the signature tree's names ride on it, and the errand routes, the session's original goal, fit as a second layer switched on from the header.
assumptions: Is GitHub as the centre right, when local copies stay on the machine until pushed?
Should the browser stay a place of its own, pending the venue-or-machine call?
Is one GitHub block enough, or should each repository get its own?
Do the errand routes belong on this picture, or on one of their own?
